sections.heading: SPHINCS Signature Lifetime Parameter
sections.summary: No consensus yet between 2^24 and 2^30 signature lifetime; benchmarks from hardware signer team expected in coming days.
sections.body:
- The group revisited the open question from the previous call about the SPHINCS signature lifetime parameter, with the main candidates being 2^24 (~16 million signatures) and 2^30.
- Matteo Vena (representing the hardware signer perspective) reiterated support for 2^24, citing:
  - An article on blockchains that he referenced mentions 2^24.
  - Institutions already rotate keys, as confirmed on the previous call.
  - Higher lifetime values degrade performance on constrained hardware and MPC implementations, potentially leaving behind millions of devices.
- Emile (Tom Wambsgans) stated he does not have a strong opinion and it depends on the performance trade-offs.
- Antonio Sanso expressed personal preference for a longer lifetime (2^30 or higher), arguing that 2^24 (~16 million) is a number small enough that users might worry about counting signatures, whereas larger values remove that anxiety.
  - He noted the original SPHINCS used 2^64, which is astronomical and worry-free.
  - He stated he starts to feel comfortable at 2^24 but would prefer higher.
- Matteo acknowledged the reasoning for bigger parameters but stressed the community must understand the trade-off: higher lifetime may exclude constrained signing devices.
- Matteo's team is working on benchmarks and potential alternative solutions, with plans to publish new work in the coming days or next week.

sections.heading: Daisugi Testnet Update and Next Steps
sections.summary: Daisugi currently runs interim Lean SPHINCS parameters; next version will deploy sphincs.art parameters on an expanded network with EthPandaOps support.
sections.body:
- Daisugi testnet is up and running with an intermediate version of Lean SPHINCS parameters chosen by the Project 11 team, not yet the sphincs.art parameters agreed upon two weeks ago.
- Antonio Sanso plans to work with EthPandaOps (Ethereum Foundation DevOps) over the next two weeks to expand Daisugi with more nodes.
- Once the bigger network is ready, the sphincs.art parameter set (agreed in the previous call) will be deployed on Daisugi.
- EthPandaOps tooling will generate fake transactions to create traffic on the testnet.
- The next call in two weeks is expected to be more substantive, with Daisugi running closer-to-final parameters on the larger network.

sections.heading: Falcon Fixed-Point Implementation on Cortex-M4
sections.summary: New fixed-point Falcon implementation on Cortex-M4 achieves ~2x of Dilithium speed (down from 4x gap), eliminating floating-point dependency; submitted to CHES 2027.
sections.body:
- Amit presented joint work with Stef and Tim from Ruhr University Bochum on an efficient fixed-point Falcon implementation for Cortex-M4, submitted to CHES 2027 (not yet peer-reviewed).
  - The ePrint preprint is available at [eprint 2026/2431](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2431).
- Background on Falcon and the GPV framework:
  - Falcon uses the GPV hash-and-sign paradigm over NTRU lattices, where signatures are short pre-images of hashed messages.
  - Key generation requires solving an NTRU equation; the secret key is a good (small-norm) basis of the lattice.
  - Falcon uses FFT-based sampling to achieve n·log(n) complexity instead of n² from naive GPV.
  - The Falcon tree (LDL decomposition of the secret key) can be precomputed or computed on the fly to minimize RAM.
- Security notes:
  - Signature security reduces to unforgeability under chosen message attack via multi-targeting homogeneity assumption.
  - Key security depends on the NTRU assumption, for which no security proof from standard assumptions exists (open problem).
  - Falcon's key generation constraints produce keys that are not perfectly Gaussian, but no attacks have exploited this.
  - Current Falcon parameters are not sufficient in the QROM model (recent result from the past year).
- The core problem: Falcon's original dependency on floating-point arithmetic.
  - Many embedded processors (e.g., Cortex-M4) lack a floating-point unit.
  - Floating-point division is not constant time, making it unsuitable for security-critical operations.
  - Masking floating-point arithmetic is an open problem; masking divisions incurs ~100x overhead.
  - Emulating floating-point with integers still incurs ~20x overhead.
  - This is likely why the Falcon standard has not been approved for the past 3 years.
- The fixed-point approach:
  - Recent work recasts Falcon's sampler security using absolute bounds, enabling control of key generation errors and bounding all intermediate values.
  - This allows a fixed-point implementation using a 32/64 format, amenable to modern processors.
  - Security loss from fixed-point conversion: only 2 bits of security.
- Key optimization: delayed rounding.
  - After each fixed-point multiplication, rescaling/rounding is normally required (10-15 cycles on Cortex-M4 per round, vs. 1 cycle for multiply-accumulate).
  - By keeping wide/buffer limbs with extra precision, rounding can be delayed to the end.
  - This enables fusing operations like inverse-and-multiply with a single final round.
  - Result: ~2x speedup in complex multiplication, ~4x for reciprocals, significantly improving FFT operations.
- Performance results (32/64 format on Cortex-M4):
  - Falcon-512: ~9.1 million cycles.
  - Falcon-1024: ~19.3 million cycles.
  - Now only ~2x slower than Dilithium (previously ~4x slower per signing trial).
  - Improved precision now allows reporting 2^99 queries, up from 2^56 which was below the NIST threshold.

sections.heading: Falcon's Role in the Ethereum Ecosystem
sections.summary: Ethereum L1 remains committed to hash-based signatures; Falcon tracked for ecosystem relevance (L2s, account abstraction), with EIP-8288 a possible future path.
sections.body:
- Antonio Sanso clarified that the PQTS group remains fully committed to hash-based signatures for Ethereum L1.
- Falcon presentations are welcome to track progress, as the broader ecosystem (L2s, account abstraction, contract-based wallets) may adopt it.
- Emile noted that EIP-8288 would allow Falcon to be used in the future.
- Gustavo mentioned a Blockstream Research article reviewing lattice-based algorithms for Bitcoin, where Falcon/FN-DSA was considered the "least worse" option.
  - It is unclear whether Amit's new results address the drawbacks Blockstream identified.
- Antonio noted that Solana has committed to using Falcon and that Falcon signature aggregation has improved in recent months.
